KEY MESSAGE 1...

A moisture-starved cold front has already cleared the forecast
area. Early afternoon observations are clear areawide, with
temperatures already in the upper 60s to mid 70s and dewpoints
ranging from the lower 40s to the lower 50s. We will continue to
mix into a dry layer aloft this afternoon with dew points
continuing to trend down. Have reduced values over central
guidance which is typically too high in this dry air aloft 
setup, especially in the shoulder seasons. Afternoon relative 
humidity should fall into the upper 20s to mid 30s in the 
lowlands and the 30s to around 40 percent in the mountains. Ten-
hour fuel moisture at several RAWS sites was already in the 6 to
10 percent range by early afternoon, so fine dead fuels and 
leaf litter are receptive, but with leaves largely still shading
the forest floor and winds remaining relatively light this is a
drying day rather than a critical fire weather day. 

Highs this afternoon reach the mid to upper 70s across the
lowlands and Metro Valley, with 60s to around 70 in the higher
terrain and upper 50s on the highest Northeast Mountain ridges.
Friday is a near-repeat under the surface high, with another
round of mixing into dry air and afternoon humidity again in the
30s for much of the area. Highs Friday land in the mid to upper
70s in the lowlands and the 60s in the mountains. 

Tonight is the better radiational-cooling setup. Winds go calm,
skies stay clear, and dewpoints are low. Lows fall into the low
to mid 40s in the lowlands, and into the upper 30s to around 40
in areas subject to cold air drainage away from major rivers.
That is several degrees colder than raw central guidance, which
holds the lower elevations near 50 degrees with mountain valleys
generally in the 40s. Valley fog is likely after midnight along
the river valleys and in other cold-air drainage valleys, as 
river temperatures remain warmer than the overlying air. The 
same setup repeats Friday night. Where fog does not form in 
protected mountain valleys, very isolated patchy frost is 
possible toward sunrise Friday. Coverage should be limited, and
this is pretty late in the growing season for a marginal event,
so will not hoist any frost advisories at this time.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Hurricane Isaias was centered about 150 nm north of the Yucatan
Peninsula, with maximum sustained winds near 75KTs and a 
central pressure near 975 mb as of the 10 AM NHC forecast 
update. It is expected to turn north and make landfall on the 
northern Gulf coast late Friday night or early Saturday, 
continuing north into Sunday morning, then eject quickly to the 
east northeast as an extratropical low Sunday into Sunday night.
Still some uncertainty as to how this evolves; expect much more
clarity after Isaias makes landfall.

A surge of tropical moisture should begin to reach the forecast
area as early as Saturday afternoon, with rain then persisting 
through at least late Sunday night as that moisture overruns the
approaching trough. A general 1 to 2 inches is expected. Any 
heavier rain focuses on the Middle Ohio Valley into the Tug Fork,
with meaningful rain shadowing west of the spine of the higher 
terrain. The heaviest rates should come late Sunday morning into
Sunday afternoon, where warm-cloud depths are deep and CAPE is 
skinny up through around H400. Antecedent conditions are dry 
and soils should take most of this primarily beneficial rain. 
Isolated high water is still possible where a heavier band sits 
on a narrow hollow or a poor-drainage spot, but a widespread 
high water is not expected. Rain tapers Sunday night into Monday
morning as the weakening system lifts toward the Atlantic, and
Monday is a brief dry break. 

The farther west and south position of the remnant low also cuts
the tornado potential relative to yesterday. The better low-
level turning stays well to our southeast. Could still see a 
narrow window of heating allowing surface based parcel ascent 
collocated with some better low level turning across the 
southern coalfields which could yield some rotating showers or 
thunderstorms Sunday afternoon. Should this materialize, the 
tornado potential would be low, but not zero.

KEY MESSAGE 3...

Southeast flow strengthens Saturday night as the remnant
circulation approaches. Forecast profiles show a 40 to 50KT 
southeast jet developing near H850 to H800 by Sunday morning. In
the immediate lee of the higher terrain, that supports 
downslope gusts of 30 to 40 mph beginning Saturday night and 
persisting through much of Sunday, mainly on the western slopes 
of the higher terrain. Central guidance does have a marginal 
signal (slightly greater than 50 percent chance) of some 
isolated 45 mph gusts where isentropic downglide of parcels 
intersects the terrain, but this should be very spatially 
limited if it occurs.
